title: They Said There Was No Price
aliases: The Reef Is in the Walls
For Something He May Not Have Done
logline: A ruined stone shrine on three terraces, with a channel of laid stone running from it down to a river, raised — tradition says — as the price of a killing that most of the surviving evidence does not record, after the monks of the day had ruled that this particular wrong had no price at all.
human_question: When I have decided to punish myself for something, what am I expecting the punishment to buy?

place.what_kind_of_place: A small ruined stone shrine of a short-lived sixteenth-century kingdom, standing on three dressed-stone terraces cut into a low spur inside a river bend, in lowland country that gets rain on nine days in ten. Nothing above the plinth courses survives: the tiled stone floor of a square chamber, the stumps and bases of its pillars, the moulded base of a railing, two guardstones at an entrance with no door, a carved water spout, and a paved channel of laid stone running from the terraces down to the water. It is not a building in use — no image, no offerings, nobody to consult — but a fenced archaeological enclosure with a gate and a signboard, reached by a turn off a main road and an old stone bridge that is itself a gazetted monument. Every account of it is an account of why it was built, and the accounts do not agree.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: The quality of the carving against the completeness of the wreck, at close range, in the kind of flat wet light that the stonework actually wants. Rain standing in the incised lines. A border of upturned petals still crisp under moss. Leaf and flower scrolls, the faces of a guardian demon in the railing base, guardstones cut with brimming pots, a water spout finished as carefully as a piece of jewellery — all of it on a building that has no walls and no roof and was, by one account, taken apart for its stone. And two carvings nobody has ever explained: an elephant tucked almost secretly into a corner of the terrace work, and a parrot on a stone of the lowest terrace, so out of keeping with everything around it that the published guess is that a carver diverted himself. Then the channel: a line of laid stone going downhill through leaf litter into the sound of water.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Water and light, and nothing else. Nobody has to be there, nothing is scheduled, no ceremony happens. What changes is wetness: rain arriving in the canopy before it reaches the ground, stone going from pale grey to almost black in seconds and back again over an hour, the cut lines of the carving filling and draining, the channel running and then not running, and the river below rising, browning and getting louder. Early mornings put mist between the terraces and the forest.
place.when_it_looks_best: Overcast, and in the first ten minutes after rain stops — which in this valley is most days of most months. The driest month is January and the wettest June, and those are two different films: January gives dependable ground and a channel with little in it, the inter-monsoon months give saturated stone, a channel with water moving in it and a loud river, at the cost of access on unmade ground. Direct sun is the one condition to avoid: it flattens the incised work the whole film depends on.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A descent, and a film of surfaces at one remove from any view. It starts on the most finished thing in the place — cut stone at the top of the highest terrace, close enough to see where a chisel changed direction — and works downhill along a line of laid stone until it arrives at a river. The building is never shown whole. There is no establishing shot, no drone, no reveal, no crowd and no figure; the camera stays low and stays still, and the piece is built out of cuts rather than moves. What it gives instead of a view is texture, water, and going down, and it resolves the way a walk resolves: the payoff is a river arriving in frame with its sound already ahead of it, and then rain starting again on the carving where the film began.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about payment. The voice gives the chronicle's accusation once and flat, gives the answer the monks of the day are said to have returned — that for this there was no atonement — and then gives the second answer, the one the stone is: an adviser's price, a building and a river brought to it. And then it gives what the sources actually hold, which is harder than the story and more useful. Remembering a wrong is not the fault; being scorched by the remembering is. People take that scorching for a virtue that thins the wrong, and the older book says flatly that it does the reverse — it defiles the mind again and again and makes a small wrong heavy. The film's own shape carries the same point: the sources pair this state with restlessness and say it cannot hold the mind on a single object, and this is a film that never once holds its subject whole.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, top terrace, rain just stopped. Water standing in the incised lines of a petal border; moss packed in the cut; the grain of the stone where a chisel changed direction. No wider frame yet, and there will not be one.
sequence.voice: Every line you are looking at was cut on purpose, by people who were paid to cut it, for a kingdom that lasted about seventy years and left almost nothing else in stone. What the accounts give as the reason is not devotion, and it is not victory. It is a price.

sequence.on_screen: Still and low. Two guardstones cut with brimming pots at an entrance that has no door; the face of a guardian demon in the moulded railing base; the water spout, finished like jewellery, discharging nothing.
sequence.voice: The later chronicle says that Rājasiṃha killed his father Māyādunnē. It says the monks were asked what could be done about it and answered that for this there was nothing — that no act would discharge it. That is the accusation and that is the answer, said once, and this film settles neither.

sequence.on_screen: The head of the channel: the spout, then the first laid stones of a cut line running away downhill and disappearing under leaf litter.
sequence.voice: Then a second answer was given. The tradition this site carries — written down, as far as anything shows, by a colonial archaeologist three centuries later — says a priest the king had brought from the Chola country told him there was a price after all: build, and bring the river to it. This is that answer, in stone. And the books have a line about a deed done because somebody advised it: being urged changes how heavy the doing feels, not what the doing is.

sequence.on_screen: The elephant tucked into a corner of the terrace stonework, so close in that it reads only on the second look. Then the parrot on a stone of the lowest terrace, alone among lotuses and demons.
sequence.voice: Nobody can say why these are here. The published guess about the parrot is that a carver got bored. Everyone who comes up this hill comes with one question, and the stone keeps answering a different one — and on that, the books are kind. Both of them say that ordinary not-knowing, about a matter you are in no position to settle, is not the doubt they are warning about [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57]. So nobody standing here unable to say whether he did it is in any difficulty at all.

sequence.on_screen: The descent begins. A series of low static frames down the channel, each a little further on: laid stone, wet leaves, a root lifting a joint, a thread of water starting to move in the bed of it.
sequence.voice: Here is what the older book actually says about paying this way. Its own example is a man who did wrong in the pride of his youth and heard the teaching only in old age [C022-P:L141]. And then it separates two things we run together: remembering the wrong is not the fault. The fault is the burning over it. Many people, it says, take that burning for a good quality that thins what they did — and it does the opposite. It fouls the mind again and again, and it makes a small wrong heavy. A wrong with no strength in it becomes a wrong with strength [C022-P:L143].

sequence.on_screen: Further down, and the cuts get shorter. Channel, a fallen course, channel, the underside of a lintel lying where it fell, channel. The building is behind us now and was never seen entire.
sequence.voice: The same book pairs this state with restlessness and counts the two of them as a single hindrance, because remorse cannot keep the mind on one object: it shows itself as unsettledness, and its thoughts are short [C022-P:L153]. That is the shape of this film. You have not been given this building whole, and you are not going to be.

sequence.on_screen: The last stones of the channel, then the river: brown, fast, loud, the far bank solid forest. Still a low camera, still no move.
sequence.voice: The shorter book fixes where this state is allowed to live. Regret arises only in the two minds rooted in aversion, only sometimes, and never in the same moment as envy or as meanness — they come one at a time [C026-P:L39]. So this is a film about one thing. It is not a portrait of a king, and a building is not a mind. The same book also says when none of these can arise at all: while the harm in the act is being seen, while shame and dread of it are awake, while the mind is resting on something good. Not resisted — not arisen [C026-M:L15].

sequence.on_screen: Back at the top, one last macro: rain starting again, filling the cut of the petal border, the stone darkening. Hold it until the rain is the only sound.
sequence.voice: Four hundred years of people have come up that channel wanting the same verdict, and this stone has never once given it. A camera cannot show which of these states is present in anybody, and none of this was ever a way of reading a person. What the books will say is narrower and it is not about him: going over it does not make it lighter. That part is addressed to whoever is still doing it.

concept_merge.why_together: C022 supplies the teaching and the site's exact subject. Pradeepika defines kukkucca as the scorching that comes afterwards over evil done and merit left undone, and gives as its principal example a man who did wrong in the pride of youth and hears the teaching in old age [C022-P:L141]; Margaya gives the same in one sentence [C022-M:L49]. Then comes the line the whole film is built on: recalling a past wrong is expressly *not* the fault, and the belief that the scorching thins the wrong is wrong — it fouls the mind again and again and makes a small wrong heavy, and brooding over merit not made produces no merit but only weakens the mind that was ready to make it [C022-P:L143]. The same source pairs the state with restlessness as a single hindrance and says it cannot hold the mind on one object [C022-P:L153], and it supplies the exemption that protects the film from becoming an accusation: ordinary uncertainty about what one is in no position to settle is not the doubt the list means [C022-P:L179]. C026 supplies the jurisdiction. The fourteen occur only in the twelve unwholesome minds and in none of the other seventy-seven [C026-P:L25]; hate, envy, stinginess and remorse only in the two hate-rooted minds; and envy, stinginess and remorse only occasionally and never in one moment together — one at a time [C026-P:L39]. Margaya then turns the whole scheme round into the one hopeful statement in it: while the harm is being seen, while shame and dread are awake, while the mind rests on the wholesome, the unwholesome mind does not arise at all [C026-M:L15]. Put on a building that is itself a payment — dressed stone on three terraces, a channel cut to a river, a priesthood brought from overseas, raised to discharge a wrong that the chronicle's own monks had said could not be discharged and that most of the surviving testimony does not record — the diagnosis stops being doctrine and becomes a description of what the camera is already looking at.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources are not offering comfort and are not offering absolution: they are making a claim about what a mind can hold. C022 alone would be an argument with nothing under it, and would tempt the film into diagnosing a dead king. C026 alone would be a classification. Together they produce the film's two refusals. Because the three companions of aversion arrive one at a time and never together, the film can be about one factor and is barred from becoming a portrait of a bad man — a person is not a state and a building is not a mind. And because the same scheme says the state simply does not arise while the harm is in view, the alternative to paying is not forgetting and not being forgiven; it is seeing. The site then hands the pairing something no analogy could: the payment is still here, beautifully cut, and the debt it was paying is not established. Everyone who walks up the channel wants the verdict, and the exemption in C022 says that wanting it and not having it is not itself a fault. What is a fault, on these sources' own account, is the grinding — and the grinding is the one thing in this story that is demonstrably still going on, four centuries later, in the literature and in the traffic up the path.

concept_links.why: Remorse is the eleventh of the fourteen, and this location is its content. Pradeepika's definition and its worked example — the scorching that comes afterwards over wrong done and merit left undone, in a man who acted in the pride of youth and heard the teaching in old age [C022-P:L141] — is the register the whole site sits in, and Margaya's one-line definition agrees [C022-M:L49]. The film is built on the digest's own most surprising line: simply recalling a past wrong is not the fault, while the self-punishing burning over it makes a small wrong heavy and drains the strength that could do good now [C022-P:L143]. Both of the digest's does_not_transfer readings are therefore refused on screen and in the same breath. 'Guilt is good for you, remorse purifies' is rejected by the source itself, and beat 8 says so; 'never feel bad about what you did' distorts it the other way, since the source separates recalling from burning and does not forbid the first. The film also uses the source's structural point — that remorse joins restlessness as one hindrance and cannot hold the mind on a single object [C022-P:L153] — as its actual cutting pattern, which is why there is no establishing shot and no whole view of the building. Two further limits are load-bearing. The digest lists as needing expert checking the claim that strong remorse can be lifted only with the help of Buddhas, paccekabuddhas or arahants [C022-P:L151], so the film makes no claim at all about what does or does not lift anybody's regret, and it does not present the building, the channel, the priesthood or the conversion as a method, a penance or a remedy. And the digest's 'questioning is a vice' line is the film's protection: both sources say ordinary uncertainty about matters one cannot settle is not the unwholesome doubt, which is specifically about the teacher and the teaching [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57], so a film whose whole subject is an unresolved accusation is filming the exempt case. Nothing here applies the word to a named person: the sources describe moments of mind, not kinds of people, and a chronicle's charge is not a diagnosis.

C026 is the association method, and it fixes where remorse can and cannot occur. The fourteen appear only in the twelve unwholesome minds and in none of the other seventy-seven [C026-P:L25]; the hate tetrad only in the two hate-rooted minds; and hate is the constant of that group while envy, stinginess and remorse are occasional and never share a moment, arising one at a time and only with aversion [C026-P:L39]. That is what keeps this film to one subject and bars it from being a character study: a moment of remorse is not also a moment of envy, and a man is not a moment. The digest's own first limit governs the whole record and is spoken in the last beat — this is a study scheme about single moments of mind, a camera cannot show which factor is present, and the film must not claim to. Its 'bad people are shameless' limit rules out the other available mistake, because the four constant factors describe every unwholesome moment in anyone and do not describe a type of person [C026-M:L15], so no historical figure here is an example of a kind of man. Its 'being pushed excuses it' limit earns a line in beat 3, because the whole tradition about this building turns on advice given to a king: prompted minds are still fully unwholesome, and prompting changes the texture of a deed rather than its quality [C026-P:L43]. And Margaya alone supplies the inversion the film ends on: while the danger in the act is being seen, while shame and dread are awake, while the mind is settled on something wholesome, the unwholesome mind does not arise at all [C026-M:L15] — which is the sources' own alternative to paying, and it is not forgetting and not absolution.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That these texts draw a line most of us do not, and draw it against us. Remembering what you did is not the problem. The grinding over it is, because they say it fouls the mind again and again and makes a small wrong into a heavy one, and because the strength it uses up was the strength that could have done something today. They do not say that guilt cleanses anybody — they say the belief that it does is mistaken. They do not say stop caring. They say the state cannot occupy a mind that is occupied by seeing the harm clearly, and that it arrives alone, so a person in it is not thereby a bad person. And they leave the viewer a specific permission: not knowing whether something happened, when you are in no position to find out, is not a fault in you.
what_must_be_real: The ruin, the carvings, the channel and the approach bridge must be filmed as they stand, in their actual condition, with nothing cleared, wetted, dressed or lit for the camera and nothing touched: this is a gazetted archaeological site and the stone is friable where the 2003 brick repairs meet the original work. No reconstruction of any kind. The alleged killing of Māyādunnē is stated once, flat, attributed to the text that carries it, never adjudicated and never reconstructed, and no frame is composed to evoke it — no blade, no blood register, no shot of a stone floor standing in for a death. The reprisals the same chronicle reports against the order, and the number of monks the Mandārampura Puvata gives, stay in the historical thread and are not spoken in the film at all: the subject here is the payment, not the retaliation, and a killing of identifiable religious that no source lets anyone verify is not something a film in this group can carry. Nobody is cast, nobody is interviewed and no historical figure is played. No worship: if anyone is found making an offering at the site, filming stops. No verdict on the king, none on his kingdom's collapse, none on his death, and no suggestion in image, edit or narration that any of it followed from what he did or did not do. The conversion and the settlement of Śaiva priests are recorded as layers of what happened, never narrated as apostasy, never as tolerance, and never as the cause of anything. Where the record is contested — the parricide, the builder, the dedication, the destruction, the meaning of the name — the film says it is contested and stops there. The tradition that the shrine was built as atonement is attributed to the tradition and to the archaeologist who wrote it down, and is never given as a chronicle's testimony, because it is not in the chronicle it is usually credited to.
position_hint: late candidate in the group: it is the film about what is left when the heat has gone out and only the account remains, and it is the one place in the group where the doctrine's subject is a physical object rather than a situation. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the film say, or let a viewer conclude, that guilt cleanses anybody — the reading the source itself rejects [C022-P:L143].
The opposite drift: implying that nobody should feel anything about what they did, when the source separates recalling, which it leaves alone, from the burning, which it does not.

Diagnosing a dead king. The scheme describes single moments of mind and a camera cannot show which factor is present; a chronicle's accusation is not a mental state and the film must never narrate Rājasiṃha as being in one.

Adjudicating the parricide by weight of sources. The temptation is real because the tally looks lopsided, but two of the sources usually counted against the charge are silent rather than contradictory, which is an argument from silence and not a denial — the record must keep that distinction.

Presenting the building, the channel, the imported priesthood or the conversion as an atonement that the sources endorse or condemn, when the digest flags the source's own claim about what lifts strong remorse as needing expert checking [C022-P:L151].

Letting the conversion become the film's explanation of anything. The record of Śaiva settlement at Buddhist centres is a layer and is recorded as one; narrated as cause, it becomes a film about religious betrayal, which is not this concept and not this project.

The chronicle puts into the king's own mouth, at his defeat, the sentence that the power of his merits had declined. It is a real quotation and it is exactly the register the floor forbids — kamma as fate, a fall as a verdict. It stays in the historical thread and does not enter the voice.
Beauty swallowing the subject. Wet carving in flat light is seductive and the film could become a piece about craftsmanship, with the argument decoration on top of it.
Making the two unexplained carvings whimsical. The elephant and the parrot are used because the building will not answer the question people bring it, not as charm.

The rival claims about who built it, what it was dedicated to and how it came down have no recorded quarrel attached to them. The film must not manufacture one, and must not turn a spread of scholarly opinion into a dispute between communities.

Naming the mountain whose revenues the chronicle says were transferred, or the hill court where the rumour circulated. Both are real places, both belong to other films on the slate, and the place-name rule covers them.
drop_if: The carvings named here — the petal border, the demon faces, the guardstones with pots, the spout, the elephant and the parrot — cannot be found or are too weathered to read, since the film is made of them and has no wide shot to fall back on.
The paved channel is no longer traceable from the terraces to the river, which is the film's spine and its only movement.
Filming inside the enclosure, or on the gazetted approach bridge, cannot be permitted without disturbing the fabric.
The site turns out to be in active devotional use, so that a film with no worship in it could only be made by asking people to stop.

connections.note: That record's historical thread already carries Rājasiṃha I's transfer of a sacred mountain's custody to Śaiva ascetics after 1581 and its reversal under Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha. The same king and the same reversal stand behind this film's question about who wrote the accusation and when; neither film names the other's place.
The hill-country campaign that ends this king's reign, and the ridge it failed at, belong to that film. This one stops at the building and keeps the campaign out of the voice entirely.
That film is inscription-led: cut letters carrying a text. Here the stone carries no text at all, which is the point — the carving is evidence of expenditure and of nothing else.
Two ways for the group to end: a crossing that will not open, and a payment made for a debt nobody can prove.

selection.reason: Remorse is the only factor in the group's concept pair that no other film carries, and this is the one place on the island where the factor exists as a building rather than as an analogy: a dressed-stone shrine and a cut channel raised, by the tradition the site carries, to discharge a wrong whose occurrence is not established. The distinction the sources draw between remembering and burning can therefore be shown without any living person being asked to admit to anything.

review.note: Rewritten whole on 2026-09-26 under the GRP-03 reassignment, and the verdict is reset to pending because the body and the location are both new. The previous film — a coral-mined coast where the reef had been burned into the lime of the village walls — was not replaced for any fault in its philosophy; its reading of C022 was sound. It was replaced because it carried the concept by resemblance, because its subject was the standing condition of a living community's livelihood, and because in a group about the hate-rooted minds a film whose engine is what identifiable people did for wages breaks the floor however carefully it is narrated. What replaces it is a place where the history is the argument rather than a likeness of it. The title changed with the film: the working title given in the reassignment, 'For Something He May Not Have Done', put the weight on the king's innocence, and the research moved the centre of the film somewhere better — the later chronicle has the monks of the day rule that this particular wrong could not be discharged at all, and the building is what was done after that ruling. Both earlier titles are kept in aliases. The district cost is stated plainly and is not disguised, and because district names are place names it is written out in suggested_location.research_note rather than here: this film leaves a district that was carrying six and enters a district that was also carrying six, which therefore reaches seven and is closed by the slate's own rule. That district is where the site is — the gazetted approach bridge lies in one of its divisional secretariat divisions, and Bell surveyed the shrine in his report on that district — and the seventh film is the stated price of taking the best doctrinal fit on the list rather than forcing a weaker location to protect a count. Nine corrections to the briefing notes are recorded in the historical thread and in the research note, the largest being that the Rājāvaliya does not contain the atonement story attributed to it: the translation has no kovil in it anywhere, and Arittakīvendu Perumāl appears once, as one of a company of fakirs from the Chola country, with no advice, no atonement and no diverted river. The story is local tradition recorded by Bell in 1904 and by Abeyawardana in 2002, and it should never again be cited to the chronicle.

suggested_location.region: Kegalle District, Sabaragamuwa Province — at Sītāvaka in Grama Niladhari Division No. 118, Pahala Thalduwa, of the Dehiovita Divisional Secretariat Division, immediately east of Avissawella across the Sītāvaka Ganga on the Avissawella–Ginigathhena road
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place found where the factor is a building rather than a comparison. C022's remorse is the scorching that comes afterwards over a wrong done, and the specific teaching the film is built on is that the scorching does not thin the wrong but makes it heavier — which means the interesting object is not a person feeling bad but a payment made in the belief that it would work. Here the payment survives and the debt does not. Three terraces of dressed stone, carving of a quality out of all proportion to the building's size, an imported priesthood, and a channel cut from the terraces down to a river: raised, by the tradition the site carries, to discharge a parricide which the later chronicle's own monks are said to have ruled could not be discharged, and which most of the surviving testimony either denies or does not mention. The place also films. It is an intimate, wet, roofless ruin in rainforest country, where flat overcast light is the correct light for incised stonework, and where the only movement in the frame is rain and river — which gives the group a film with no drone, no wide view, no crowd and no figure in it, built as a descent along one cut line. Nothing else considered for this concept offered the doctrine and the pictures in the same object.

historical_thread.story:
Sītāvaka was a kingdom of about seventy years in the sixteenth century, and the shrine known as Berendi Kovil is the best-preserved piece of stone architecture left from it. The archaeological account is short and firm. The site consists of three levels, with the kovil on the upper one: a rectangular building rising from a paved basement, built in the manner of South Indian Vijayanagara work, with carved water spouts, volute balustrades, moonstones, dressed slabs and door-frames, flower and leaf carving on the base stones, bahirava faces in the moulded railing base, a border of upturned petals, two guardstones carved with what read as full pots, and an elegantly cut water spout. A canal paved with stones links the kovil to the Sītāvaka Ganga. Two carvings are unexplained: an elephant cut almost secretly into a corner of the terrace stonework, and a parrot on a stone of the lowest terrace, so distinct and so out of place that the published suggestion is that the sculptor diverted himself. H. C. P. Bell conserved the site in 1895 and described it in his Report on the Kegalla District, printed in 1904 (pp. 63–65); short earlier notices exist from Percival (1800), Forbes (1827), H. White, C. J. R. Le Mesurier (1885) and F. H. Price (1887). The Department of Archaeology conserved the stonework again in 2003, replacing damaged parts in brick. The stone bridge on the way to the kovil, in Grama Niladhari Division No. 118 Pahala Thalduwa of the Dehiovita Divisional Secretariat Division, was declared a protected monument by gazette notification No. 1486 of 23 February 2007, p. 128.

The story attached to the building is a story about atonement, and its transmission is the most interesting thing on the site. Bell in 1904 and Abeyawardana in 2002 record it as local tradition: that Rājasiṃha I of Sītāvaka built the shrine after embracing Śaivism, in an effort to escape the consequence of having killed his father Māyādunnē, and that Arittakīvendu Perumāl, the priest said to have converted him, guided the building of it. Bell also derives the name from 'Berendu Kovil', which he glosses as the temple to get redemption. A widely reproduced travel article adds the detail on which the site's popular fame rests — that when the guilt came upon the king he asked his adviser what could atone for it, and was told the only way was to build a kovil by diverting the river — and attributes that account to the Rājāvaliya. It is not in the Rājāvaliya. B. Gunasekara's translation of that chronicle contains no kovil at all; Arittakīvendu Perumāl appears in it exactly once, as one of a company of fakirs who had come from the Soli country, appointed Mannamperuma Mohotti and given 'the daughter of the Rajahetti, who had been the king's concubine' — not the king's daughter — after which he becomes a general and the chronicle follows him to the end of the kingdom. There is no guilt, no consultation, no atonement and no diverted river in it. Nor does the Rājāvaliya contain the parricide: where Māyādunnē's death falls, it says only that 'King Mayadunne died after he had reigned 70 years', with no cause and no accusation.

The accusation is carried by the later chronicle. The relevant chapter stands in the section of the Cūḷavaṃsa added after chapter 90 — Geiger noted that the manuscripts themselves mark a break there — and the part covering this reign is attributed to Tibbotuwawe Sri Siddhartha Buddharakkhita, writing under Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha (1747–1780), some hundred and sixty years after the events. Malalasekera's Dictionary of Pāli Proper Names summarises the passage, at Cv. xciii.3ff., thus: Rājasīha was king 1581–93, son of Mayadhanu, with his capital at Sītāvaka; 'he slew his father, and, when the monks declared that it was impossible to atone for such a heinous crime, he turned against them, gave the revenues from Sumanakuta to the Saivite priests, slew the monks, and burned their sacred books.' The Minor Rājāvaliya is also cited for the monks having judged the act an anantarika kamma, an offence of immediate and unalterable result, and for the quarrel with the order that followed. The Mandārampura Puvata reports that 121 monks were killed in one place. What the king did religiously is recorded independently of the charge: he took up Śaiva Siddhānta, made Arittakīvendu his chief adviser with the title Mannamperuma Mohoṭṭala, and settled Brahmans and Tamil Śaiva Vellālas at major Buddhist centres, among them the island's great mountain of pilgrimage, whose custody was not returned to the order until Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha's reign.

Against the charge stand three different kinds of evidence, and they are not of equal weight. Fernão de Queyroz, a Portuguese Jesuit with no sympathy for this king, wrote at length about him and reported that Māyādunnē died of natural causes after living eighty-five years — a positive denial, and the only one. João Ribeiro does not record a parricide. The Rājāvaliya and the Alakeśvara Yuddhaya do not record it either, and the standard argument in the literature is that these two, being Sinhala works close to the period, would have said so had it happened; that is an argument from silence, and it is repeatedly reported as though it were testimony. Finally, the Dutch emissary Joris van Spilbergen, received with ceremony at the hill capital in May 1602, reported that the parricide rumour was circulating only in that kingdom — and the man receiving him was Vimaladharmasūriya I, formerly Konappu Bandāra, son of Vīrasundara Bandāra, whom Rājasiṃha I had appointed to govern the hill country, then suspected of disloyalty and had killed. The accusation, in other words, is first attested circulating in the one court with the clearest motive to circulate it, and is first written down under the king who reversed Rājasiṃha's religious settlement.

The end of the reign is in the Rājāvaliya and is worth having straight, because it is usually reported as a simple accident. After the failure of the hill-country campaign the king withdrew to a park at Petangoda, and there 'a bamboo splinter ran into the king's foot'. The chronicle immediately adds that the astrologer Dodampe Ganitaya, by influence of magic, prevented the poison of the wound from being extracted, and that prince Rāja Sūrya brought magical influence to bear on it; a few pages later it states outright that Rāja Sūrya caused the king's death by getting the astrologer to practise witchcraft. The king was carried away by royal barge and died without speaking again. The chronicle dates the death to the expiry of 1514 years of the Śaka era and to a Thursday, the seventh day of the lunar month, under the asterism Hata. Geiger's own chronological table gives the reign as 1581–1593 and converts the chronicle's Śaka figure to 1592/3; popular accounts give March 1592 and 17 March 1593 with equal confidence. The modern suggestion that the cause was tetanus is a hypothesis about the wound, not a report from any source.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concept asks a single question — what is a person doing when they try to settle a past wrong by suffering over it — and this site answers it in the most literal available material, then complicates the answer in exactly the way the sources do.

First, the building is the mistake C022 names, at the scale of a state. Pradeepika is unusually direct here: the scorching over what one did is taken by many people for a good quality that thins the wrong, and it does the reverse — it fouls the mind again and again, and a wrong that had no strength in it acquires strength [C022-P:L143]. Here somebody acted on the belief the source rejects, and the acting is still standing: three terraces of dressed stone, carving of a quality out of all proportion to the building, a priesthood brought from overseas, and a channel cut to fetch a river. Whether it worked is not a question a film can put; whether the source thinks that kind of payment works is not in doubt at all. And the chain the later chronicle gives is the doctrinal chain in narrative form: the monks are asked and answer that for this there is no atonement; a different adviser supplies one; the building follows. The film does not need to say that the monks were right. It only needs to show what was built after they had said there was nothing to build.

Second, the debt is not established, and that is the site's real gift rather than a weakness in it. Pradeepika separates remembering from burning and leaves the remembering alone [C022-P:L143], and both sources rule that ordinary uncertainty about something one cannot settle is not the doubt the list means [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57]. A place where four centuries of visitors have wanted a verdict and not got one is therefore the exempt case, filmed as the exempt case — and it makes the film's only accusation land somewhere safe. What is demonstrably going over and over this one alleged act is not the dead king. It is the literature, and it is the traffic up the path, and the camera is the newest arrival in that queue. That is where the group's charge belongs: on the looking, not on anybody in frame.

Third, the transmission history is the same shape as the doctrine and is the part that could not have been invented. The accusation is not in the chronicle closest to the events; it appears in a continuation written some hundred and sixty years later, under the king who undid the religious settlement it condemns, and it is first attested as a rumour in the court of a man whose father the accused had had killed. The tradition that the building was an atonement is later still — the earliest attestation found for it is a colonial archaeologist's report of 1904 — and the chronicle it is universally credited to does not contain it. So the record in front of the camera is a payment of unknown purpose, wrapped in a charge of uncertain origin, wrapped in an explanation supplied by the people who came to look. Every layer of it was added by somebody going over the story again.

Fourth, C026 stops the film from becoming the thing the floor forbids. Because remorse arises only in the two hate-rooted minds, only occasionally, and never in the same moment as envy or stinginess — one at a time [C026-P:L39] — a moment is not a man, and this cannot be a portrait of a bad king; the film is about one factor and says so. Because the four constants describe every unwholesome moment in anybody and not a type of person [C026-M:L15], no historical figure here is an exhibit. Because prompting changes a deed's texture and not its quality [C026-P:L43], the fact that the whole tradition turns on advice given to a king neither excuses nor aggravates anything, and the film says that once and moves on. And because the same source says the unwholesome mind does not arise at all while the harm in the act is being seen, while shame and dread are awake, while the mind rests on the wholesome [C026-M:L15], the film has an ending that is neither absolution nor despair: the alternative to paying was never forgetting, and it was never being forgiven. It was seeing.
what_is_certain: Berendi Kovil is a ruined Hindu shrine at Sītāvaka, in the Kegalle District, dated to the middle of the sixteenth century by Bell (1904). It is described as one of the major surviving archaeological monuments of the Sītāvaka kingdom (1521–1593).

The site consists of three levels, with the kovil on the upper level; the building is rectangular and rises from a paved basement. Its recorded features are carved water spouts, volute balustrades, moonstones, dressed stone slabs and door-frames, flower and leaf carvings on the base stones, bahirava faces, a border of upturned petals round the base of the structure, two guardstones carved with what appear to be full pots, and a moulded railing base around the pillars of the upper terrace (Bell 1904; amazinglanka's site description).
A canal paved with stones links the kovil to the Sītāvaka Ganga (Abeyawardana 2002, as reported by Lankapradeepa).

Two carvings at the site are recorded as unexplained: an elephant carved into a corner of the terrace stonework, and a parrot on the stone wall of the first (lowest) terrace. The parrot is independently reported by the Sabaragamuwa provincial tourism site as an engraving on one of the foundation stones.

H. C. P. Bell conserved the site in 1895 and described it in Report on the Kegalla District of the Province of Sabaragamuwa, Archaeological Survey of Ceylon XIX–1892, printed 1904, pp. 63–65. Short earlier notices are attributed by Bell to Percival (1800), Forbes (1827), H. White, C. J. R. Le Mesurier (1885) and F. H. Price (1887). The Department of Archaeology conserved the stonework again in 2003, using brick to replace damaged parts.

The stone bridge on the way to the kovil, in Grama Niladhari Division No. 118 Pahala Thalduwa of the Dehiovita Divisional Secretariat Division, is a protected monument declared by gazette notification No. 1486 of 23 February 2007, p. 128. Pahala Thalduwa is a Grama Niladhari Division of Dehiovita, which is the fourth largest Divisional Secretariat of the Kegalle District.

Bell (1904) and Abeyawardana (2002) record as local tradition that Rājasiṃha I built the shrine after embracing Hinduism, in an effort to escape the consequence of having murdered his father Māyādunnē, and that Arittakīvendu Perumāl, the priest said to have converted him, guided its construction.
Bell (1904) records the name as a corruption of 'Berendu Kovil', which he glosses as 'the temple to get redemption'.

The Rājāvaliya, in B. Gunasekara's translation, records Aritta Kivendu Perumāl once: he was one of some fakirs who had come from the Soli country, was appointed Mannamperuma Mohotti, was given 'the daughter of the Rajahetti, who had been the king's concubine', and became a great favourite of the king, later commanding armies and surviving the kingdom's fall.
The Rājāvaliya records Māyādunnē's death in one sentence — 'King Mayadunne died after he had reigned 70 years' — with no cause stated and no accusation made.

Malalasekera's Dictionary of Pāli Proper Names, s.v. Rājasīha, citing Cūḷavaṃsa xciii.3ff., gives the charge in full: he was king 1581–93, son of Mayadhanu, his capital at Sītāvaka; 'he slew his father, and, when the monks declared that it was impossible to atone for such a heinous crime, he turned against them, gave the revenues from Sumanakuta to the Saivite priests, slew the monks, and burned their sacred books.'

The chapter carrying that charge falls in the part of the Cūḷavaṃsa added after chapter 90 — Geiger's own note records that the manuscripts mark the break at 90.102 — and the continuation covering this reign is attributed to Ven. Tibbotuwawe Sri Siddhartha Buddharakkhita, writing in the reign of Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha (1747–1780).

Rājasiṃha I took up Śaiva Siddhānta, appointed Arittakīvendu his chief adviser with the title Mannamperuma Mohoṭṭala, and is reported to have settled Brahmans and Tamil Śaiva Vellālas at significant Buddhist sites, the mountain of pilgrimage among them; Buddhist custody of that mountain was restored under Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha.

Fernão de Queyroz, author of The Temporal and Spiritual Conquest of Ceylon and hostile to this king, reported that Māyādunnē died of natural causes after living eighty-five years. João Ribeiro records no parricide. The Rājāvaliya and the Alakeśvara Yuddhaya do not mention one.

The Dutch emissary Joris van Spilbergen was received at the hill capital in May 1602 by Vimaladharmasūriya I and is reported to have recorded that the parricide rumour was circulating only in that kingdom.

Vimaladharmasūriya I was Konappu Bandāra, son of Vīrasundara Bandāra, whom Rājasiṃha I had appointed to govern the hill country after his 1582 invasion, then suspected of disloyalty and had killed; Konappu fled to Portuguese territory, was baptised at Goa as Dom João de Áustria, returned, and became king of the hill country in 1592.

The Rājāvaliya's account of Rājasiṃha I's death: after the failure of the hill-country campaign he withdrew and was carried to the park at Petangoda, where 'a bamboo splinter ran into the king's foot'; the astrologer Dodampe Ganitaya 'by influence of magic prevented the poison of the wound from being extracted', and prince Rāja Sūrya 'brought magical influence to bear upon the wound'. He was brought away by royal barge and died without speaking again. The same chronicle later states that Rāja Sūrya caused the death by getting the astrologer to practise witchcraft.

The Rājāvaliya dates the death to the expiry of 1514 years of the Śaka era, on a Thursday, the seventh day of the lunar month, under the asterism Hata. Geiger's chronological table gives the reign as 1581–1593 and converts the chronicle's Śaka figure to 1592/3.

Avissawella, the nearest town, has a tropical rainforest climate: about 2,262 mm of rain a year falling on some 289 days, wettest in June (about 341 mm), driest in January (about 40 mm), with the heaviest periods April to June and September to November.
what_is_disputed: Whether Rājasiṃha I killed his father. This is the centre of the film and it is not resolved here. The correction that matters to the record is that the balance of testimony is usually misreported: only Queyroz positively denies it, saying Māyādunnē died naturally at eighty-five. Ribeiro does not mention it, and the Rājāvaliya and Alakeśvara Yuddhaya do not mention it; the standard argument that those two 'would have said so' is an argument from silence and is not a denial, though it is repeatedly reported as if it were one. On the other side stand the later Cūḷavaṃsa at xciii.3ff., the Minor Rājāvaliya's report that the monks judged the act an anantarika kamma, and the rumour Spilbergen found circulating in 1602. Two facts about the accusation's carriers are established and are not an argument against it: the chronicle was written under the king who reversed Rājasiṃha's religious settlement, and the court where the rumour circulated was headed by the son of a man Rājasiṃha had killed.

The briefing note for this film, and much of the site literature, attribute the atonement account to the Rājāvaliya. That attribution is wrong. Gunasekara's translation of the Rājāvaliya contains no kovil, no atonement, no consultation about guilt and no diverted river, and it records Arittakīvendu Perumāl only as a fakir from the Soli country raised to office. The earliest attestation found for the atonement story is Bell's report of 1904, which gives it as local tradition; Abeyawardana (2002) repeats it. The 'diverting the river' detail reaches the internet through a Daily Mirror travel article reproduced on amazinglanka, which credits the Rājāvaliya for it. The story is tradition and must be attributed to tradition.

Whom Arittakīvendu Perumāl married. The Rājāvaliya says the daughter of the Rajahetti, who had been the king's concubine. The travel account says the king's own daughter. The English Wikipedia article says a sister of a junior queen. Three versions, one chronicle sentence.

Who built the shrine. The prevailing view credits Rājasiṃha I (1581–1593); some credit his father Māyādunnē (1521–1581); one popular account says it was standing before Rājasiṃha's time, within the Sītāvaka period. A further unattributed claim holds that the style of the stone columns, railings and floral and leaf motifs is Polonnaruwa-period work; no scholar is named for it, and the same site literature elsewhere calls the building South Indian Vijayanagara work. The two attributions are not reconcilable and neither is sourced to a named study here.

To whom it was dedicated. Lankapradeepa, following the site literature, says Kālī (given as 'Kali Yakshani'); the Sabaragamuwa provincial tourism site says the deity was Śiva and gives Kālī as local folklore; the Wikipedia account of the king describes his religion as Śaiva Siddhānta. Not settled.

How the building came down. The archaeological account, via Bell and Abeyawardana, is that after the shrine was abandoned its materials were dismantled to build other nearby constructions. The travel account says the Portuguese destroyed it. These are different claims and the record does not choose between them.

The meaning of the name. Bell derives it from 'Berendu Kovil', the temple to get redemption. A rival derivation, given without authority, reads it as Bhairava-aṇḍi kovil, from the bahirava faces on the building. Both are etymologies offered long after the fact.

The date of the king's death. Geiger's table gives the reign as 1581–1593; the Rājāvaliya's own reckoning, the expiry of 1514 Śaka, converts to 1592/3; popular accounts state March 1592 and 17 March 1593 with equal confidence. The film states no date.

Two figures in the tradition do not survive their own arithmetic. The Rājāvaliya says Māyādunnē 'died after he had reigned 70 years', where his conventional dates of 1521–1581 give sixty. Queyroz says he died having lived eighty-five years, where a birth in 1501 and a death in 1581 give seventy-nine or eighty. Neither figure is used.

The number of monks killed. The Mandārampura Puvata reports 121 in one place; secondary accounts speak of hundreds of prelates executed after a conspiracy was exposed. The film states no number and does not reconstruct the episode.

Whether this is 'the only stone monument surviving from the Sītāvaka kingdom'. The claim is common in travel writing; the archaeological literature says only that it is one of the major surviving monuments of that kingdom, and the palace and fort site at Pahala Maniyangama in the same Divisional Secretariat Division is separately gazetted. Not used as fact.

Which district the site is in, as the sources report it. The gazette entry, Bell's Kegalla District report and Lankapradeepa all place it in the Kegalle District of Sabaragamuwa; amazinglanka places it in the Colombo District and the Western Province tourism board lists it as a Western Province destination. The site lies immediately across the Sītāvaka Ganga from a town that is in the Colombo District, which is the likely source of the confusion. It does not appear on the Colombo District list of protected monuments and it does appear on the Kegalle one. This record uses Kegalle.

What exactly is protected. The item gazetted on 23 February 2007 is the stone bridge on the way to the kovil, not the kovil itself; whether the shrine carries a separate declaration under earlier legislation was not established.

Whether the channel is a canal, a moat, or both. Abeyawardana describes a stone-paved canal linking the kovil to the river; the provincial tourism account says the river encircles the site on three sides and that a stone bridge 4.6 m across on the western side shows where a moat ran, with smoothed stone suggesting steps down from the bridge toward the temple. The tradition's 'diverting the river' may describe either.

Parricide is a recurring narrative model in the Sri Lankan chronicle tradition, treated at length by Gananath Obeyesekere in The Work of Culture (Chicago, 1990) under the chapter 'Myth models of the parricide: Oedipus in Sri Lanka', which also discusses an earlier royal case. That is a reason to handle a late chronicle's parricide charge with source criticism; it is not evidence about this king, and nothing is inferred from it here. The chapter was not read for this record.

The chronicle puts a sentence into the king's mouth at the point of defeat — that he had fought since his eleventh year, that no king had stood before him, that the man now in the hill country was a favourite of fortune, and that the power of his own merits had declined. It is genuine chronicle testimony and it is recorded here. It is deliberately kept out of the film, because narrating a reign's collapse as merit running out is precisely the kamma-as-fate reading the project's floor forbids.

what_to_film: The incised carving at macro range in flat wet light, with rain standing in the cuts: the border of upturned petals, the leaf and flower scrolls on the base stones, the bahirava faces in the moulded railing base, the volute balustrade.
The two guardstones with their full pots, filmed at the entrance they guard, which has no door and no building behind it.
The carved water spout, close, discharging nothing.
The elephant tucked into the corner of the terrace stonework, and the parrot on the stone of the lowest terrace, both found and framed without pointing — the film needs them to be nearly missable.

The paved stone channel in sequence from its head on the terraces down to the river, as a run of low static frames rather than a move, including the places where roots and fallen courses interrupt it.
The tiled stone floor of the upper chamber and the pillar stumps, from ground level, in rain.
The 2003 brick repairs against the sixteenth-century stone, honestly, as the condition of the site.
The old stone bridge on the approach, filmed end-on, and the water under it.
The river itself after rain: brown, fast and loud, with the far bank forest, as the film's arrival.
The same carving twice, wet and dry, so that the stone's change under rain reads without narration.
suggested_location.access: By road: a signposted turn off the Avissawella–Ginigathhena road a short distance east of Avissawella, just past the bridge over the Sītāvaka Ganga, with a Department of Archaeology signboard and a gate into the enclosure. About 52 km and roughly an hour and a half from Colombo. The site is a declared archaeological area and the approach bridge is a gazetted protected monument, so filming, any equipment placed on the fabric, and drone use over the enclosure all need Department of Archaeology permission; none has been sought. The terraces are reached on foot up a short slope that is slippery in rain, and the channel runs downhill over unmade, leaf-covered ground to the river. No permission, access arrangement or local contact has been obtained for any part of this.
suggested_location.best_time: Overcast, and in the minutes after rain stops, which is common here through most of the year. January is the driest month and is the safer choice for ground conditions and for working on the slope, at the cost of a channel with little water in it. The inter-monsoon months of April to June and September to November give saturated stone, water moving in the channel and a loud river, and worse footing. Early morning for mist between the terraces and the forest. Direct midday sun is the one condition to avoid outright, because it flattens the incised carving the film is made of.

images.caption: The wet-zone forest country of the Sītāvaka valley, photographed in the botanical garden a few kilometres west of the site. This is NOT the monument and shows none of it: it is included only for the vegetation, the light and the rainfall the film has to work in. Wikimedia Commons holds no photograph of Berendi Kovil.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 26 September 2026, and nine corrections to the briefing notes are recorded rather than smoothed. (1) The atonement story is not in the Rājāvaliya. B. Gunasekara's translation was downloaded and read in full: the word kovil does not occur in it, Arittakīvendu Perumāl occurs once as a fakir from the Soli country appointed Mannamperuma Mohotti, and there is no guilt, no consultation, no atonement and no diverted river. The story is local tradition, first attested in Bell's report of 1904 and repeated by Abeyawardana (2002); the 'diverting the river' version reaches the web through a Daily Mirror travel article that credits the chronicle wrongly. (2) The Rājāvaliya does not deny the parricide either — where Māyādunnē's death falls it says only that he 'died after he had reigned 70 years', with no cause. So the briefing's 'most of the surviving testimony denies the parricide' overstates: only Queyroz denies it, two Sinhala works are silent, and the standard case against the charge is an argument from silence. (3) The chronicle locus of the charge is Cūḷavaṃsa xciii.3ff., not 'Mahāvaṃsa Chapter 4'; and the Cūḷavaṃsa, not only the Minor Rājāvaliya, carries the monks' ruling that the act could not be atoned for, together with the transfer of the mountain's revenues, the killing of monks and the burning of books. That ruling is now the film's centre and the reason for the new title. (4) Who wrote it and who carried it are both documentable and both new to this record: the chapter stands in the continuation added after Cūḷavaṃsa 90.102, attributed to Tibbotuwawe Sri Siddhartha Buddharakkhita under Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha (1747–1780), the king who restored Buddhist custody of the mountain Rājasiṃha had given to Śaiva priests; and the Kandyan court where Spilbergen found the rumour in 1602 was headed by Vimaladharmasūriya I, son of the Vīrasundara Bandāra whom Rājasiṃha I had had killed. (5) The death date is not firm. Geiger's table gives 1581–1593 and converts the Rājāvaliya's Śaka 1514 to 1592/3; the briefing's 'March 1592' is one of two dates in circulation, the other being 17 March 1593, and both are stated with equal confidence in popular sources. Both are recorded; neither is used. (6) The bamboo splinter is only the first half of the chronicle's account of the death: the Rājāvaliya immediately adds that an astrologer magically prevented the poison from being drawn and that a prince worked magic on the wound, and later says outright that the prince caused the death by witchcraft. The tetanus explanation is modern hypothesis. (7) Two figures in the tradition fail their own arithmetic — the Rājāvaliya's seventy-year reign for Māyādunnē against conventional dates giving sixty, and Queyroz's eighty-five years of life against a birth in 1501 and a death in 1581. (8) 'The only stone monument surviving from the Sītāvaka kingdom' is travel-writing phrasing; the archaeological literature says one of the major surviving monuments, and the palace and fort site at Pahala Maniyangama in the same Divisional Secretariat Division is separately gazetted. (9) What was gazetted on 23 February 2007 (Gazette 1486, p.128) is the stone bridge on the way to the kovil, in GN Division No. 118 Pahala Thalduwa, Dehiovita DS; whether the shrine itself carries a declaration was not established. The district was checked rather than assumed: the gazette entry, Bell's Kegalla District report and Lankapradeepa put the site in Kegalle District, Sabaragamuwa; amazinglanka says Colombo District and the Western Province tourism board lists it as a Western Province destination; it is absent from the Colombo District protected-monuments list and present on the Kegalle one, and the site lies immediately across the river from a town that is in Colombo District, which explains the error. Kegalle is used. The district cost, stated here rather than in the review note because district names are place names: the film leaves Galle District, which falls from six films to five, and enters Kegalle District, which rises from six to seven and is thereby closed under the slate's own rule that seven or more is closed. That is the stated price of taking the best doctrinal fit on the list instead of forcing a weaker location to protect a count, and Kegalle is simply where this monument is. What could not be verified: Bell 1904 pp. 63–65 was not read — the Zenodo scan is 140 MB, has no OCR and is missing pages — so everything attributed to Bell comes through Lankapradeepa's citations of him; Abeyawardana 2002 p.67 likewise. Queyroz was not read: the Internet Archive copy of the English translation is lending-restricted and no scholarly edition was reachable, so his statement about a natural death at eighty-five is reported from secondary summary only. Cūḷavaṃsa xciii.3ff. was not read in Geiger's translation either: chapters 92 to 95 are absent from the available scan, and the passage is quoted here from Malalasekera's Dictionary of Pāli Proper Names, s.v. Rājasīha, which cites it. The Minor Rājāvaliya, the Alakeśvara Yuddhaya and the Mandārampura Puvata were not consulted at all and are reported at second hand; the Alakeśvara Yuddhaya is described in the literature as a late-sixteenth-century 'floating text' with an unstable manuscript tradition, which weakens any argument from its silence, and Alan Strathern's source-critical article on it was not obtained. Obeyesekere's chapter on parricide as a narrative model was not read. Coordinates are Lankapradeepa's (6.955228, 80.224154) and were not independently checked against a survey sheet or against the enclosure boundary. Nothing about permissions, drone rules over a declared archaeological area, the present legibility of the channel from the terraces to the river, or the current condition of the named carvings has been verified on the ground. Images: the Commons search API was queried with a descriptive user agent across eighteen terms in English, Sinhala and Tamil transliteration, including the monument's name and its variants, the kingdom, the district, the divisional secretariat, the river and the nearest town. Commons holds no photograph of Berendi Kovil — the only hits on its name were scanned volumes of the Journal of the Ceylon Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society. The single image carried here is of the wet-zone forest of the same valley, taken in a botanical garden a few kilometres west of the site, confirmed to exist by action=query&titles=File:Seethawaka_Wet_Zone.jpg&prop=imageinfo, and its caption says explicitly that it is not the monument. A photograph of the surviving stone was deliberately not substituted from another site, and nothing unconfirmed is linked.

unknowns: No permission has been sought from the Department of Archaeology for filming inside a declared archaeological area, for placing any equipment near the fabric, or for flying over it — and the film as written needs no drone, which removes one of those requests but not the others.

Whether the paved channel can still be followed on foot and on camera from the terraces to the river is the question that decides whether the film has its spine; it is reported in the literature and has not been checked since.

Whether the specific carvings the film is built from — the petal border, the bahirava faces, the guardstones with pots, the spout, the elephant and the parrot — are still legible after two conservation campaigns and a century of rainforest weathering.

Whether the site sees devotional use. Nothing found suggests it does, but a ruined kovil with a name meaning redemption is the kind of place where offerings appear, and a film with no worship in it cannot be made by asking anyone to stop.

Bell 1904, Abeyawardana 2002, Queyroz, the Cūḷavaṃsa chapter itself, the Minor Rājāvaliya, the Alakeśvara Yuddhaya and the Mandārampura Puvata were all reported at second hand. The film's central chain — the monks' ruling that no atonement was possible — rests on a reference-work summary of a chapter that could not be read.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified; the historical thread is desk research by web search and by reading one chronicle translation in full, with everything not read marked as such in the research note. No scene or shot is decided here.
